title: Would a Quebecor-Telus merger mean higher cellphone bills for Canadians?
summary: Quebecor says its proposal to acquire one of the four main Canadian telecoms will lead to lower costs for consumers, but policy analysts and competition advocates aren't quite buying it.

image.caption: President and CEO of Quebecor Pierre Karl Péladeau looks on during the company's annual general meeting in Montreal in May 2025. (Christopher Katsarov/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Quebecor says its proposal to acquire one of Canada's four main telecoms will lead to lower costs for consumers, but policy analysts and competition advocates aren't quite buying it.

When Montreal-based telecom Quebecor announced Monday it wanted to buy Telus for $31 billion, its pitch touted greater efficiency, "pro-consumer pricing" and strengthened Canadian digital sovereignty.

"The proposed combination will create a Canadian-controlled competitor, fully integrated from coast to coast, capable of investing more and offering consumers more choice, healthy competition and real value," Quebecor said in a news release.

But the overture is the first major telecom merger proposal since Canada tightened competition regulations following its 2023 approval of Rogers's buyout of Shaw. If the deal is ultimately approved, Canada would go from four to only three major telecommunications companies.

"What it means for consumers is less, less, less when it comes to choice, and more and more and more when it comes to prices," said Keldon Bester, executive director of the Canadian Anti-Monopoly Project.
Will rates go down if Quebecor buys Telus? | Hanomansing Live

Following the Rogers-Shaw merger, Bester says companies can no longer justify an anti-competitive merger simply by arguing it would generate cost savings, and mergers that exceed market concentration thresholds are now presumed to harm competition unless the companies prove otherwise.

Quebecor also faces restrictions since it acquired Freedom Mobile in 2023, including limits on transferring spectrum licences until 2033. These changes could make Quebecor's proposed takeover of Telus considerably harder to approve than the Rogers–Shaw deal.
In response to the "unsolicited" proposal, Telus raised concerns, noting it had identified "significant regulatory and execution risks associated with the proposed Quebecor transaction."

items: Quebecor makes $31B offer to acquire Telus

blocks.text: The company — overseen since July by former CIBC CEO Victor Dodig — said it had formed a special committee to explore Quebecor's overture as well as "other strategic alternatives available to Telus to maximize value for the company and its stakeholders."
Quebecor had a strong year, outpacing competitors on the stock market. Meanwhile, Telus's stock has seen a steady decline.
Telus reviewing $31B takeover offer from Quebecor

Federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly released a statement saying she would not predetermine the outcome of a regulatory review by the Competition Bureau and the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC).
The minister's statement echoed some of the claims made by Quebecor, noting that "connectivity is critical to Canada’s economy, sovereignty and national security."
Prime Minister Mark Carney said more competition, lower prices and better service would be key to any decision regarding the telecom sector.
Speaking in China, where he is attending the APEC summit, Carney was asked about Quebecor's proposed takeover of Telus.

Carney declined to comment directly on the proposal, but said that under certain circumstances and depending on the market structure, an oligopoly situation can lead to more competition with fewer players, though he didn't elaborate further.
To Bester, the government's language wasn't encouraging.
He described the prospect of the acquisition as a potential return to the "bad old days" before the emergence of independent competitors such as Wind Mobile, which eventually became Freedom.

Quebecor President and CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau waits to speak at the Freedom Mobile Arch concert venue ahead of its inaugural event at the Pacific National Exhibition grounds, in Vancouver, in June 2026. (Darryl Dyck/CBC)
Bester said the consequences could be particularly significant given that Canada has only recently begun to see improvements in wireless affordability.
"We appear to have been in a honeymoon period," he said, referring to the competition that followed the Rogers-Shaw merger.
He warned that those improvements shouldn't become an argument for allowing the market to consolidate again.
From 4 to 3 major telecoms
Freedom Mobile's acquisition by Quebecor in 2023 was a key condition of Ottawa's approval of the Rogers-Shaw merger, intended to preserve a fourth major competitor in Canada's wireless market.
Since then, Freedom has expanded its offerings and put pressure on the country's largest providers to lower their prices.
Bryson Masse, a telecommunications policy consultant, said Quebecor's proposal risks reversing that progress.
He pointed to the company's own presentation, which describes plans to position Freedom as an "anchor brand" within the combined business.
Masse says that would leave Freedom operating as a discount brand owned by one of the country's largest telecommunications companies, rather than an independent challenger competing against it.
"When there's one less company chasing for your business, the other two don't have to work as hard," Masse said. "And that has an effect on price."
Jennifer Quaid, a competition law expert at the University of Ottawa, said concerns about higher cellphone bills are justified, although the impact would likely vary across the country.
"I think consumers are obviously … concerned rightly that at least based on intuitive sense of going from four to three that there's gonna be less pressure on those big players," she said.

In some cities, Quaid said, consumers may still have access to smaller providers offering competitive plans. In others, there may be few alternatives to the country's largest telecommunications companies.
The question is also whether a merger puts a company in a position where it can do so without facing meaningful competition.
Why does Canada lack competition in so many industries?
Making it easier for independents to access networks
Both Masse and Bester argued that regulators have other tools available to encourage competition and reduce cellphone bills without allowing another major telecommunications merger.
One is expanding the rules that allow smaller wireless providers to offer services using infrastructure owned by larger companies.

Canada's current wholesale access framework allows eligible regional providers to use the networks of established telecommunications companies, but generally requires them to invest in building their own network infrastructure.

Bester said those restrictions make it unnecessarily difficult for smaller companies to enter the market. He believes opening up the networks more broadly would allow additional competitors to offer lower prices without having to build new infrastructure.
Masse said Quebecor's own submissions to the CRTC have advocated for measures to prevent large providers from charging competitors more for network access than they charge their own retail customers.
Such measures could help smaller providers compete without requiring the multibillion-dollar acquisition of an existing telecommunications giant, Masse said.
Bester believes Quebecor shouldn't have to buyout Telus in order for Canadian companies to be able to offer lower prices.
"We can do that without sacrificing a fourth player," he said. "It's totally unnecessary."
